chapter: The 1949 band, breakup and later years
title: Against fixed personnel and overplaying soloists
summary: Barnet prefers writing for individuals as Ellington did and criticizes soloists who play everything in eight bars, including Thad Jones-Mel Lewis.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: didn't approach the cohesion and the organization and the -- well, they just weren't organized like the older bands had been, and I like the idea of a constant personnel. I don't like this idea of -- and of course, as the band business matured and got on and on -- you can say matured, or maybe it got -- went the other way, I'm not sure. The idea of a fixed personnel, it became ridiculous. You had a parade of people going through a band, I mean, -- all -- the arranger became to the point where he wasn't writing for individuals anymore, he was writing for a group of people that played exactly this way and no other way, and if you didn't play that way you were a misfit. And I was unhappy with this, because I always believed -- I thought the Ellington theory was the best way. Write for the guys, the individual. And it became impossible to have a white band where you could have a constant personnel. And you can't be writing for people that are not there. So this became a question of a mob scene, writing arrangements for a bunch of guys, you know, anybody that comes along, which makes it very indistinct. Any wide interpretation of anything would be out of line, because the background that was written for any solos denied this. And also, there was a tendency in all of the soloists, every time they got ahold of eight bars it was like the Third World War. In other words, they never -- I used to tell them, "Why don't you listen to what's going on behind you? Listen to the

background. Now play something in there that fits. Don't, the minute it says ad lib solo, don't start playing the Arbens book, just because you've got eight bars or sixteen bars to shine. Listen to what's going on around you and try to fit something beautiful into that." This was gone, this was all gone. And I find -- I take umbrage with the Thad Jones-Mel Lewis Band with this. They're going along, they've got a beautiful arrangement going, and all of a sudden some guy will come in with a solo, I mean, and just destroy the whole damn mood. It's like he's got to play everything he ever knew in his life, I mean, in that one outing. Now, this to me is wrong. I think I better get off the soapbox here.
That's all right,hey. That's what -- you know, this is for -- this is your forum.
